questions.questionText: Why do cybercriminals frequently target Virtual Assistants (VAs) in executive impersonation attacks?

options.text: VAs are responsible for writing all company software code.
VAs possess administrative access, schedule control, and are socialized to respond rapidly to executive commands.
VAs do not use internet connections.
VAs are legally responsible for company tax payments.

questions.explanation: VAs hold central administrative access and high-level trust, making them high-value targets (Lazarus, 2024).

questions.questionText: An email from a CEO requesting that a Virtual Assistant purchase $1,000 in Apple gift cards for a "client emergency" is almost certainly a social engineering scam.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Requesting gift card purchases is a primary financial scam tactic; legitimate businesses do not use gift cards for emergency corporate transactions.

questions.questionText: You receive a message on Telegram from your remote boss: "I am on a plane with no voice signal. Send me the MFA code that was just sent to your phone so I can access my email." What should you do?

options.text: Send the MFA code immediately via Telegram.
Do not send the MFA code. MFA passcodes must never be shared, and the request is a credential interception attempt.
Post the MFA code on LinkedIn.
Email the code to the entire company.

questions.explanation: MFA tokens grant account access and must never be shared, even if the requester claims to be an executive.

questions.questionText: Which of the following elements are red flags indicative of executive impersonation? (Select TWO)

options.text: The sender instructs you NOT to call them to verify the request because they are "in an urgent meeting."
The request arrives via an official internal ticketing system with manager approval.
The message comes from a personal webmail address like ceo.companyname@gmail.com.
The request asks you to follow standard, documented procurement policies.

questions.explanation: Prohibiting voice verification and using external webmail accounts are classic executive spoofing indicators.

questions.questionText: Threat actors use psychological authority pressure to make Virtual Assistants feel that questioning an executive's request will lead to immediate firing.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Fear of disciplinary action is manipulated to force VAs to bypass security checks.

questions.questionText: What is "Out-of-Band (OOB) Verification" in the context of Virtual Assistant workflows?

options.text: Verifying a request using a different, independent communication method than the one used to send the request.
Replying to an email using ALL CAPS.
Sending a text message to the same scammer.
Deleting your email inbox.

questions.explanation: OOB verification confirms identity via a separate, trusted channel (e.g., calling a known phone number).

questions.questionText: You manage the calendar for a remote Vice President. An external consultant emails asking you to add a Zoom link to the VP's calendar for a "confidential acquisition meeting." The email attachment is Meeting_Agenda.docm. What should you do?

options.text: Open the attachment and click "Enable Macros" to see the agenda.
Do not open the attachment; verify the meeting request directly with the VP or your internal team lead before updating the calendar.
Share the VP's personal home address with the consultant.
Forward the file to your personal family members.

questions.explanation: Unsolicited macro-enabled files (.docm) are common malware delivery vectors.

questions.questionText: What term describes an attacker flooding a Virtual Assistant's phone with dozens of login push notifications late at night in hopes the VA will tap "Approve"?

options.text: Credential stuffing
Push Bombing / MFA Fatigue Attack
Port Scanning
SQL Injection

questions.explanation: MFA fatigue exploits distraction and frustration to coerce push approvals.

questions.questionText: If an executive texts you from a new, unverified phone number claiming they lost their device, you should immediately grant them full access to all company cloud drives without secondary verification.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Identity must be independently verified through official channels before granting access from new devices.

questions.questionText: Why do pretexters impersonating executives create artificial time emergencies ("Need this done in 15 minutes before board meeting")?

options.text: To help the Virtual Assistant finish work early.
To induce panic and reduce the VA's time to perform critical verification checks.
To reduce internet server usage.
Because executives cannot wait more than 15 minutes for anything.

questions.explanation: Artificial time pressure suppresses analytical thinking and security protocol adherence.
